newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND-S American oil producers to shine in 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-S American oil producers to shine in 1997.

text.p: Look for South America's oil producers to give a voluminous performance in 1997, but don't expect regional powerhouse Venezuela to steal the show.

Industry analysts say Venezuela will begin to share the spotlight with Brazil and Colombia next year and Argentina will slip to understudy status, as the region continues to enjoy the fruits of deregulation and privatization.
Excluding Venezuela, South American output should grow by 10.5 percent to 3.56 million barrels per day (bpd) in 1997, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA) in Paris.

"Deregulation is the name of the game," says Eduardo Fernandez, associate director for the Latin American team at Cambridge Energy Research Associates near Boston. "All these countries need money for exploration and production, and that money won't come from governments."
In its forecast, which excludes countries like Venezuela that are part of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), the IEA predicts Brazil will get top billing.
But make no mistake, Venezuela is still the region's diva, with plans to pump over 500,000 bpd more in 1997, including crude, natural gas liquids and equivalent barrels of natural gas.

Still, Brazilian output, fueled by surging activity on deep-water offshore rigs, should climb by 220,000 bpd next year, the IEA says. Total production averaged about 900,000 bpd last month, heading toward a goal of one million bpd by end-1997, and 1.5 million bpd in the year 2000, according to state-owned Petrobras.

Brazil is also expected to make progress next year on regulations to implement a constitutional reform aimed at relaxing Petrobras's current monopoly, which will open the floodgates to pent up private-sector upstream investment.
"Brazil has 160 million people, and has a significant participation in Southern Cone demand," CERA's Fernandez said, referring to the southern half of South America.
"Everyone is looking there to extend their markets," he said. "What is not clear is how far the government will go with deregulation," Fernandez said.
Petrobras, which is seeking to retain its grip on the country's most promising areas, will have three years to tap prospective fields before opening up to the private sector.

"In the meantime, we may see a joint venture with 20 percent or 30 percent going to a private company, but that's not the most attractive investment. Companies want to operate," says Rafael Quijano, director of Washington, D.C.-based Petroleum Finance Co.
"Petrobras is just coming out of the denial period on this process," says Quijano.
Quijano contends that Colombia, no stranger to foreign investment, could upstage Brazil next year.
The giant Cusiana and Cupiagua fields, operated by British Petroleum, will move toward peak levels of 500,000 bpd next year, up from around 180,000 bpd now, once new pipeline facilities are in place.

The IEA predicts Colombian flows to climb by an average 120,000 bpd next year, up from a total of nearly 626,000 bpd in 1996, with 79 percent coming from association contracts with private companies, according to state-owned Ecopetrol.

Venezuela too is banking on privatization, hoping foreign investment will help state-owned Petroleos de Venezuela SA realize its ambitious 10-year plan to reach 6.2 million bpd of total liquids capacity in 2006.
According to official figures, PdVSA plans to produce 3.71 million bpd of hydrocarbons next year, up some 500,000 bpd from 1996.
Industry sources note that while Venezuela denies allegations it exceeds its current OPEC output quota of 2.359 million bpd, it is likely counting on the demise of the system.
"The entire PDVSA plan for the future assumes there is no quota system because everyone is producing at capacity," says Wolf Petzall, a Caracas-based consultant.
"The increase will come largely from tremendous drilling efforts in established areas like Lake Maracaibo," says Petzall, referring to Venezuela's traditional oil heartland.

Some of the fresh flows will also come from old fields revitalized by private companies. Firms operating under 14 existing contracts now pump around 180,000 bpd, and could reach 400,000 bpd in 2000, analysts say.

A new tender for 20 more so-called marginal areas is already underway. PDVSA plans to announce the names of companies that have been pre-qualified to bid beginning February 3, with final bidding planned for the end of May, PDVSA officials say.
Other regional producers get mixed reviews from analysts. Argentina, plagued by a low ratio of reserves to production, not likely to improve much on its current output of around 790,000 bpd.
"Argentina's production has gone up every year, but reserves haven't increased," says Petroleum Finance Co's Quijano. "Production in 1997 is going to be level, or plus or minus five percent."

The IEA meanwhile forecasts that Ecuador will add another 20,000 bpd to its current output of about 385,000 bpd, while a combined 10,000 bpd will come from minor regional producers such Trinidad and Tobago, Bolivia, Chile and Barbados.
